section.heading: 5.2. Logarithmic Functions
Logarithms
section.paragraph: You are already familiar with exponential equations of the form
$${b^{y} = x} \left( {b > 0,b \neq 1} \right)$$

where the variable $$x$$ is expressed in terms of a real number $$b$$ and a variable $$y$$ . But what about solving this same equation for $$y$$ ? You may recall from your study of algebra that the number $$y$$ is called the logarithm of $$\mathbf{x}$$ to the base $$\mathbf{b}$$ and is denoted by $$\mathbf{\log_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{x}}$$ . It is the power to which the base $$b$$ must be raised to obtain the number $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe that the logarithm $$\log_{b}x$$ is defined only for positive values of $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: The two most widely used systems of logarithms are the system of common logarithms , which uses the number $$10$$ as its base, and the system of natural logarithms , which uses the irrational number $$e = 2.71828\ldots$$ as its base. Also, it is standard practice to write log for $$\log_{10}$$ and ln for $$\log_{e}$$ .
The system of natural logarithms is widely used in theoretical work. Using natural logarithms rather than logarithms to other bases often leads to simpler expressions.

section.paragraph: One easy way to obtain the graph of the logarithmic function $$y = \log_{b}x$$ is to construct a table of values of the logarithm (base $$b$$ ). However, another method—and a more instructive one—is based on exploiting the intimate relationship between logarithmic and exponential functions.
If a point $$(u,v)$$ lies on the graph of $$y = \log_{b}x$$ , then
$$\nu = \log_{b}u$$
But we can also write this equation in exponential form as

So the point $$(v,u)$$ also lies on the graph of the function $$y = b^{x}$$ . Let’s look at the relationship between the points $$(u,v)$$ and $$(v,u)$$ and the line $$y = x$$ (Figure 7). If we think of the line $$y = x$$ as a mirror, then the point $$(v,u)$$ is the mirror reflection of the point $$(u,v)$$ . Similarly, the point $$(u,v)$$ is the mirror reflection of the point $$(v,u)$$ . We can take advantage of this relationship to help us draw the graph of logarithmic functions. For example, if we wish to draw the graph of $$y = \log_{b}x$$ , where $$b > 1$$ , then we need only draw the mirror reflection of the graph of $$y = b^{x}$$ with respect to the line $$y = x$$ (Figure 8).

section.paragraph: You may discover the following properties of the logarithmic function by taking the reflection of the graph of an appropriate exponential function (Exercises 33 and 34).

note.title: Properties of the Logarithmic Function
note.heading: Properties of the Logarithmic Function
note.paragraph: The logarithmic function $${y = \log_{b}x}\left( {b > 0,b \neq 1} \right)$$ has the following properties:

list.item: Its graph passes through the point $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ .
It is increasing on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b > 1$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b < 1$$ .

section.heading: Properties Relating the Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
section.paragraph: We made use of the relationship that exists between the exponential function $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ and the logarithmic function $$g(x) = \ln x$$ when we sketched the graph of $$g$$ in Example 6. This relationship is further described by the following properties, which are an immediate consequence of the definition of the logarithm of a number.

section.paragraph: (Try to verify these properties.)
From Properties 2 and 3, we conclude that the composite function satisfies

$$\begin{array}{rcll} {\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x)} & = & {f\left\lbrack {g(x)} \right\rbrack} & \\ & = & {e^{\ln x} = x} & \left( { \text{for all} x > 0} \right) \\ {\left( {g \circ f} \right)(x)} & = & {g\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack} & \\ & = & {\ln e^{x} = x} & \left( { \text{for all} x > 0} \right) \end{array}$$

Any two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ that satisfy this relationship are said to be inverses of each other. Note that the function $$f$$ undoes what the function $$g$$ does, and vice versa, so the composition of the two functions in any order results in the identity function $$F(x) = x$$ .*
For a more extensive treatment of inverse functions, see Appendix A.
The relationships expressed in Equations (2) and (3) are useful in solving equations that involve exponentials and logarithms.
